result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_spectrum()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the adjacency matrix. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L48255-L48402){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_spectrum( which="largest", k=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Adjacency spectrum](/assets/graphs/get-spectrum.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node graph and a bar chart of its five adjacency eigenvalues, sorted from largest to smallest: 2.641, 0.724, -0.589, -1.000, and -1.776. The largest eigenvalue is in the accent color." width="100%"} Returns the spectrum (eigenvalues and eigenvectors) of the graph's adjacency matrix. The spectrum reveals important structural properties including connectivity, bipartiteness, and graph regularity. The adjacency matrix follows the same conventions as NetworkX: edge weights are used when present (otherwise `1.0`), parallel edges sum their weights, and an undirected self-loop adds its weight once to the diagonal. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [which]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["largest"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which eigenvalues to return: - `"all"`: all `n` eigenvalues - `"largest"`: the largest `k` eigenvalues - `"smallest"`: the smallest `k` eigenvalues For directed graphs, "largest" and "smallest" are by real part. [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of eigenvalues to return for `"largest"`/`"smallest"`. Default is `min(6, n)` where `n` is the number of nodes. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary with keys: - `"values"`: list of eigenvalues, sorted descending - `"vectors"`: list of unit eigenvectors aligned with `"values"`; entry `j` of each vector belongs to node `nodes[j]` - `"nodes"`: node IDs, in creation order, giving the order of eigenvector entries - `"spectral_gap"`: `λ₁ - λ₂` over the full spectrum (`None` for a single node) For directed graphs the adjacency matrix is not symmetric, so `"values"` holds Python `complex` numbers sorted by real part, and `"vectors"` and `"spectral_gap"` are `None`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is empty, `which` is invalid, or the eigenvalue computation fails to converge. ::: ## Common Use Cases {.doc-common-use-cases} - spectral clustering: community detection via eigenvectors - graph embedding: represent nodes using eigenvector coordinates - bipartite detection: check if spectrum is symmetric about `0` - random walk analysis: eigenvalues determine mixing time - graph comparison: compare spectral distributions ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The adjacency spectrum captures a graph's global structure in a bounded list of real numbers, and many core properties are recoverable directly from it. The *spectral radius* $\rho(A) = \max_i |\lambda_i|$ satisfies $\rho(A) \le \Delta(G)$ and hits that bound exactly for regular graphs, where every eigenvalue is bounded above by the shared degree. The *spectral gap* $\lambda_1 - \lambda_2$ quantifies expansion, and a zero gap witnesses disconnection. Bipartiteness reveals itself as spectrum symmetry about the origin, since a graph is bipartite iff its adjacency spectrum equals its negation as a multiset. Signature spectra include $K_n \to \{n - 1, -1, \ldots, -1\}$, the cycle $C_n \to \{2\cos(2\pi k / n)\}_{k = 0}^{n - 1}$, and the star $S_n \to \{\sqrt{n - 1}, 0, \ldots, 0, -\sqrt{n - 1}\}$. For undirected graphs with at least 400 nodes, `"largest"` and `"smallest"` with a small `k` use a sparse iterative solver (Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration) that touches only the graph's edges, so they scale to graphs with hundreds of thousands of nodes (a few seconds for 200,000 nodes). It is a block method, so it resolves repeated eigenvalues, which are common in graph spectra. Results match the dense solver to about `1e-11` relative to the spectral radius. Convergence slows when the requested eigenvalues are tightly clustered relative to the spread of the whole spectrum. Everything else runs a dense $O(n^3)$ eigendecomposition: `"all"`, small graphs, and directed graphs (Francis double-shift QR). This is practical up to a few thousand nodes. Eigenvector signs are normalized so that the first non-negligible entry is positive, making results reproducible. ## Examples {.doc-examples} **Spectral Analysis of Complete Graph** A complete graph `K_5` has a very distinctive spectrum: one large eigenvalue of `n-1` and the rest equal to `-1`, which produces a large spectral gap: ::: {#115ba275 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes([f"v{i}" for i in range(5)]) g.add_edges([(f"v{i}", f"v{j}") for i in range(5) for j in range(i+1, 5)]) spec = g.get_spectrum(which="all") # Returns [4.0, -1.0, -1.0, -1.0, -1.0] spec['values'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [4.000000000000002, -0.9999999999999996, -1.0, -1.0, -1.0] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#30f37a7d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Returns 5.0 (largest minus second-largest eigenvalue) spec['spectral_gap'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 5.000000000000002 ``` ::: ::: **Detecting Bipartite Structure** A bipartite graph's spectrum is symmetric around zero -- the largest and smallest eigenvalues are mirror images of each other: ::: {#a019b8fb .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) # Left partition: A, B; right partition: X, Y, Z g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "X", "Y", "Z"]) g.add_edges([("A", "X"), ("A", "Y"), ("B", "Y"), ("B", "Z")]) spec = g.get_spectrum(which="all") values = spec['values'] # Returns True: the spectrum is symmetric about zero, a signature of bipartiteness abs(values[0] + values[-1]) < 0.01 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: ::: **Directed Graphs Have Complex Spectra** A directed cycle's adjacency matrix is a permutation matrix, so its eigenvalues are the roots of unity. They are returned as complex numbers sorted by real part: ::: {#9f2eb052 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A")]) # Returns 1, ±i, and -1 (the fourth roots of unity) [complex(round(v.real, 6), round(v.imag, 6)) for v in g.get_spectrum(which="all")["values"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [(1+0j), 1j, -1j, (-1+0j)] ``` ::: :::
